prompt: Where does the planner get the numbers behind a `rows=` estimate?
hint: It does not look at the rows themselves.

choices.text: From a summary ANALYZE made from a sample
choices.why: Right: pg_stats shows that summary, made from 30,000 rows at the default target.

choices.text: From a quick count of the matching rows at planning time
choices.why: Counting would cost as much as the query; the planner never counts.

choices.text: From the times the last runs took, in pg_stat_statements
choices.why: The planner does not read the tally; it is a separate extension.

choices.text: From the index, which stores how many rows hold each value
choices.why: A B-tree stores entries, not a count per value, and many columns have no index at all.

prompt: `pg_stats` shows `n_distinct = -1` for `orders.placed_at`. What does the planner take that to mean?
hint: A negative number is not a count.

choices.text: The column has no statistics yet, because ANALYZE has not reached it
choices.why: Missing statistics mean no row in pg_stats at all, not a negative value.

choices.text: Every row has a value of its own, at any table size
choices.why: Right: a negative n_distinct is a fraction of the rows, and -1 is all of them.

choices.text: The column has exactly one value, the same one repeated in every single row
choices.why: That would be n_distinct = 1, a positive count.

choices.text: The values are in descending order on disk
choices.why: Order on disk is the correlation column, and placed_at's is 1.

prompt: Why does `pg_stats` hide the rows of columns the user cannot select?
hint: Think about what most_common_vals holds.

choices.text: Because reading statistics is slow and it saves time to skip them
choices.why: The view is tiny; the filter is about who may see it.

choices.text: Because only the planner is allowed to read statistics
choices.why: Anyone may read pg_stats for columns they can select, as this lesson does.

choices.text: Because the summary holds real values copied out of the table
choices.why: Right: the common values and the histogram bounds are data, and would leak it.

choices.text: Because pg_statistic is stored encrypted for every role but the owner
choices.why: Nothing is encrypted; superusers read pg_statistic directly.

prompt: With `default_statistics_target` at 100, how many rows does ANALYZE sample from each table?
hint: 300 rows per unit of the target.

prompt: Seller 42 is not on the list of common values. How does the planner estimate its orders?
hint: What is left after the listed values?

choices.text: It splits what the list leaves evenly
choices.why: Right: 0.7382 shared by 990 sellers, times two million, is 1491.

choices.text: It uses the frequency of the least common value on the list
choices.why: That would give about 2333; the plan said 1491.

choices.text: It reads the histogram bounds of seller_id
choices.why: For an equality on a value off the list, the leftover share is what is used.

choices.text: It counts seller 42's rows in the index
choices.why: The planner never counts; the estimate is arithmetic on the summary.

prompt: Seller 553 was second on the list at 0.0013666666 and got an estimate of 2733, but has 1590 orders. What would most likely bring its estimate closer?
hint: Why was it on the list at all?

choices.text: Raising the column's statistics target, so a bigger sample tells chance from frequency
choices.why: Right: it was listed by the luck of a 30,000-row sample; a bigger one shrinks that noise.

choices.text: Creating an index on seller_id
choices.why: The index already exists and plays no part in the estimate.

choices.text: Setting n_distinct to 1000
choices.why: It already is 1000; listed values ignore n_distinct anyway.

choices.text: Running VACUUM FULL on orders
choices.why: Rewriting the table changes no statistics.

prompt: Seller 1 is estimated at 501,600 orders and seller 42 at 1491, and both get a bitmap scan. Where does the difference in their estimates still matter?
hint: Look at the costs, and think of a bigger query.

choices.text: Nowhere, since both got the same plan and a plan is all that runs
choices.why: The costs differ, 28,585 against 4,497, and costs drive every choice above the scan.

choices.text: Only in the time EXPLAIN takes to print
choices.why: EXPLAIN took under a millisecond for both.

choices.text: In the cost, which decides the joins built on top
choices.why: Right: inside a bigger query, the row count drives everything built on top.

choices.text: In the size of the index the bitmap scan has to read from disk
choices.why: The index is the same for both; only how much of it is read differs.

prompt: `status` has four values and all four are on its list of common values. How is `status = 'pending'` estimated?
hint: Nothing is left over for an average.

choices.text: One quarter of the rows, since there are four values
choices.why: That ignores the list, which says pending is 0.0033.

choices.text: From the histogram of status
choices.why: A column whose values all fit the list has no histogram left.

choices.text: By counting the pending rows during planning
choices.why: The planner never counts rows to plan.

choices.text: Its frequency on the list times the table's two million rows: 6600
choices.why: Right: 0.0033 × 2,000,000, against 7319 real.

prompt: How does the histogram PostgreSQL keeps for `placed_at` differ from one you would draw by hand?
hint: Compare the first bucket with the last.

choices.text: It has one bucket per month
choices.why: Months would be equal widths; these buckets go from 101 days to 5.6.

choices.text: Its buckets hold equal rows, not equal time
choices.why: Right: a hundred buckets of 1% each, narrow where orders are dense.

choices.text: It stores a count of the rows for every distinct timestamp it saw
choices.why: It stores only 101 bounds.

choices.text: It covers only the most recent hundred days
choices.why: Its bounds run from January 2023 to December 2025.

prompt: A query asks for orders between 10:00 and 11:00 on one day. The day sits inside a bucket about six days wide. What does the estimate assume?
hint: The section's one assumption about a bucket.

choices.text: That the hour holds one per cent of the table, one bucket
choices.why: A whole bucket spans six days; the hour is a small slice of it.

choices.text: That the rows are uniform over those six days, so one hour gets one hundred and forty-fourth of them
choices.why: Right: about 1/144 of the bucket's 20,000 rows, whatever the hour's real traffic.

choices.text: That the hour holds the bucket's average of a whole day
choices.why: The interpolation is by time, so an hour gets a twenty-fourth of a day's share.

choices.text: That nothing happens at night, so daytime hours get more
choices.why: The histogram knows nothing about hours of the day inside a bucket.

prompt: `placed_at` has 101 histogram bounds and 2,000,000 rows. About how many rows does one bucket hold?
hint: 101 bounds make how many buckets?

prompt: About 106,000 orders by `placed_at` got a plain index scan costed at 3,913; about 103,000 by `customer_id` got a bitmap scan costed at 19,228. Which statistic explains the gap?
hint: Not how many rows, but where they are.

choices.text: n_distinct
choices.why: Both columns return about the same number of rows; distinctness is not what differs.

choices.text: null_frac
choices.why: Neither column has nulls.

choices.text: most_common_freqs
choices.why: Neither condition is on a listed value; both are ranges.

choices.text: correlation
choices.why: Right: 1 for placed_at, whose rows sit together on disk, and 0.0064 for customer_id.

prompt: Why did ANALYZE estimate about 1.44 million distinct orders in `order_lines` when there are 2 million?
hint: How often does a sample of 30,000 rows catch a second line of the same order?

choices.text: Some orders have no lines and were left out
choices.why: Every order has lines; count(DISTINCT) gave exactly two million.

choices.text: The sample saw most orders once, and guessed low
choices.why: Right: the guess from a sample errs towards too few for a column of small repeated groups.

choices.text: Statistics were stale after the load
choices.why: market.sql ends with VACUUM ANALYZE; the table has not changed since.

choices.text: n_distinct is rounded to two significant figures
choices.why: It printed -0.28848767, with eight.

prompt: A column's estimate is wrong because of a ratio your schema guarantees, say three rows per parent forever. Which fix is the lesson's recommendation, and why?
hint: One fix samples more; the other states the answer.

choices.text: SET STATISTICS 10000, because a sample big enough always finds the true count
choices.why: At 1000 it was still 16% short; a bigger sample improves distinct counts slowly.

choices.text: SET (n_distinct = -0.3333): a fixed fraction stays right as rows are added
choices.why: Right: and write down why, since nothing checks it if the ratio ever changes.

choices.text: An index on the column, so the planner can count it
choices.why: The planner does not count through indexes when it plans.

choices.text: Running ANALYZE more often
choices.why: Each run takes another sample of the same size and makes the same kind of guess.

prompt: To make ANALYZE keep more common values and more histogram buckets for one column, write `ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c SET ___ 1000;`.
hint: The same word as the server-wide default's name, without the prefix.

prompt: Curitiba is 0.0685 of the customers and PR is 0.0685. Why did the planner expect 938 for both together?
hint: What does it do with two selectivities?

choices.text: It multiplied the two fractions
Its statistics for city were out of date after the load
choices.why: Each fraction was right; the error is in combining them.

choices.text: It used the smaller of the two fractions, to be safe
choices.why: That would have given 13,700, close to the truth.

choices.text: PR is not on the state column's list
choices.why: It is, fourth, at 0.0685.

prompt: After `CREATE STATISTICS ... (dependencies, mcv) ON city, state`, a report still gets a bad estimate for `GROUP BY city, state`. What is missing?
hint: Groups are a count of combinations.

choices.text: An ANALYZE of the whole database, since one table is not enough
choices.why: The object belongs to customers; analysing that table was enough for the WHERE estimate.

choices.text: An index on (city, state)
choices.why: An index does not tell the planner how many groups there are.

choices.text: The ndistinct kind, which counts the distinct combinations
choices.why: Right: with it the estimate went from 108 to 12.

choices.text: A higher statistics target on both columns
choices.why: Each column alone is already exact; the problem is their product, 12 × 9.

prompt: `pg_stats_ext` shows `"4 => 5": 1.000000` and `"5 => 4": 0.421733`. What do they say?
hint: 4 and 5 are column positions.

choices.text: City fixes state; state rarely fixes city
choices.why: Right: SP and RJ each have several cities.

choices.text: City and state are equal in 100% and 42% of the rows
choices.why: The values are never equal; a dependency is about one predicting the other.

choices.text: The object covers columns 4 to 5 with 42% of the table sampled
choices.why: The sample is 30,000 rows; the numbers are degrees of dependency.

choices.text: A city has 1 state on average and a state 0.42 cities
choices.why: These are not averages; a state cannot have under one city.

prompt: Match each field of `pg_stats` to what it fed in this lesson.
hint: One estimate per field.

pairs.right: the groups of a GROUP BY
the cost of reading by index in order

prompt: Put the planner's arithmetic for seller 42 in order.
hint: From the list to the plan.
items: Add up the frequencies on the common-values list: 0.2618
Subtract from 1 to get what is left: 0.7382
trap: Multiplying by the rows comes last; the fraction is built first.

prompt: Which of these would `CREATE STATISTICS` on the right pair of columns help? Choose all that apply.
hint: It fixes the combining step, not a single column.

choices.text: WHERE postcode = ... AND city = ..., estimated far too low
choices.why: Right: a postcode predicts its city, and the multiplication undercounts.

choices.text: GROUP BY product_id, category with too many groups expected
choices.why: Right: the ndistinct kind counts the real combinations.

choices.text: WHERE seller_id = 553 estimated 72% high
choices.why: One column, a sampling accident: that is SET STATISTICS's job.

choices.text: An estimate that is wrong because ANALYZE has not run since a big load
choices.why: Stale statistics are fixed by ANALYZE, lesson 6's subject.

prompt: A table of sensor readings has `sensor_id` and `site_id`, and every sensor belongs to one site. `WHERE site_id = 7 AND sensor_id = 70` is estimated at 3 rows and returns 900. What do you do first?
hint: Is either column alone wrong?

choices.text: Raise default_statistics_target for the whole server
choices.why: A bigger sample keeps each fraction right and still multiplies them.

choices.text: Create extended statistics on the pair of columns, then ANALYZE
choices.why: Right: the sensor fixes the site, the same shape as city and state.

choices.text: Set n_distinct on sensor_id
choices.why: The problem is the combination, not how many sensors there are.

choices.text: Drop the condition on site_id from the query
choices.why: It would fix this estimate by changing the question; the planner's blind spot stays for every other query.
